title: A Fist Pump in Assembly
author: Lynsey White
summary: White opens with her daughter Alice, who treasures a headteacher's fist pump in assembly far more than the points or prizes. She uses it to argue that recognition for vulnerable pupils is about shifting attribution, not handing out rewards. Children with an external locus of control credit success to luck or an adult's mood, so staff should linger a few seconds and ask what the pupil did that worked. She says this work should be shared across the whole staff rather than residing in post-incident conversations or point systems. The piece closes with reflective questions for senior leadership and pastoral teams.
points: Alice remembered the headteacher's split-second fist pump, a relational connection, rather than the prize she won.
Vulnerable pupils often hold an external locus of control and attribute success to luck or an adult's good mood.
Recognition should coach the internal narrative by asking pupils to talk through what they did, rather than simply praising or awarding points.
Whole-staff reinforcement matters so a child's success is not attributed solely to one adult who likes them.
Leaders should train adults to catch micro moments and ask whether positive relational intelligence travels as fast as negative behavioural data.
quotes: Alice did not walk away from that assembly talking about the chocolate in her pocket. She walked away holding onto a split second moment of relational connection: He looked right at me. He did the fist pump.

If we want to move these children away from transactional compliance and toward authentic self belief, we have to recognise that recognition is not about handing out items or chasing points. It is about actively shifting their attribution, coaching the internal narrative of a child who does not yet know how to own their wins.
if a child has just told you they did well because their teacher was in a good mood, it’s worth staying with them for a few seconds longer.
Sometimes that starts with a question as simple as, “You reckon she was in a good mood? Talk me through what happened when you went in.” Then I need to give them time to answer.
There’s a part of the story they’ve missed, and it’s the bit they can take into maths after break. That’s where a whole staff can make a difference.
None of this changes a child’s internal script overnight. If you’ve spent years putting a good lesson down to luck, it takes a lot to say, even to yourself, “Actually, I did that.
Does positive relational intelligence travel as fast as negative behavioural data?
